sources.description:
I am an LLM researcher working on optimization and efficient training of neural networks. My current research includes low-rank pretraining, spectral regularization, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, and reducing the memory cost of language-model training.

I study how optimization and regularization affect the singular-value spectra and effective rank of weight matrices. I am interested in spectral weight decay, nuclear-norm regularization, proximal methods, and Newton-Schulz approximations. A central question is whether training can make a model easier to compress with low-rank factorization while preserving its quality. Related questions concern generalization and memorization under label noise.

Another research direction is optimization for LoRA and other low-rank parameterizations. Relevant topics include Muon-style matrix updates, optimization of factorized weights, rebalancing, spectral constraints, and convergence analysis. I want to understand both the geometry of these updates and their practical behavior when fine-tuning language models.

I also work on memory-efficient LLM pretraining. Relevant methods include low-rank gradient and optimizer-state representations, GaLore, Frugal-style methods, and low-precision optimizer states such as FP8. I am interested in their tradeoffs between model quality, training memory, throughput, and communication cost, including how those tradeoffs change with model scale.

As a secondary current interest, I am building an AI research digest agent with a handwritten harness. Relevant work includes explicit context management, structured LLM decisions, application-controlled tools, and paper retrieval and relevance ranking using lexical or embedding-based methods.

I have not specified hard topic exclusions for this digest.

passages.text: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) enables parameter-efficient fine-tuning but can suffer from redundant basis directions. Constraining the basis factor to the Stiefel manifold addresses this redundancy through orthonormality. Landing methods allow temporarily infeasible iterates to explore a neighborhood of the manifold while progressively restoring orthogonality without per-step retractions. To improve optimization efficiency while retaining this flexibility, we introduce ProLand (Product-space Landing), a retraction-free optimizer that combines coordinated factor updates with Muon-style spectral directions. By designing the updates in the space of the represented weight increment, ProLand separates objective optimization from orthogonality restoration, supporting efficient feasibility recovery. This coordinated construction also enables Muon-style directions to guide objective optimization while preserving that separation. Experiments cover four GLUE validation tasks on DeBERTa-v3-base and seven language benchmarks on Qwen2.5-3B, Llama-3.2-3B, and Moonlight-16B-A3B across multiple adapter ranks. Across these 11 tasks, ProLand achieves the highest average score among the compared methods in every tested encoder and decoder model–rank configuration.

First, coordinated updates in the product space support rapid feasibility recovery. We design the joint first-order change D B ​ A + B ​ D A D_{B}A+BD_{A} in the represented weight increment and realize it through factor directions satisfying B ⊤ ​ D B = 0 B^{\top}D_{B}=0 , even when B B is infeasible. This condition makes the optimization step leave B ⊤ ​ B B^{\top}B unchanged to first order and eliminates its first-order interaction with the Landing correction. Consequently, the optimization step perturbs the constraint violation only at second order in its step size. Under the conditions of Section 4 , this violation contracts geometrically toward a neighborhood whose radius is quadratic in that step size. This provides a mechanism for recovering feasibility while continuing to optimize the represented weight increment. Second, Muon-style directions guide objective optimization. passages.text: A growing body of work reports benefits from orthogonality constraints in fine-tuning large language models (LLMs). These results raise an open question: do orthogonality constraints also help LLM pre-training? We conduct a systematic empirical study of decoder-only LLM pre-training with models ranging from 360M to 3.1B parameters, trained on nearly 200B tokens. We examine fourteen variants of orthogonality training: some constrain the weight matrix itself, while others use orthogonal factors to reparameterize it. Because a strictly orthogonal square matrix loses half of its degrees of freedom, we also study block-wise orthogonality, where every d d rows form a row-orthonormal (Stiefel) matrix and the block size d d is a hyperparameter. Among block sizes ranging from 1 to the shorter side of the matrix, no d > 1 d>1 used throughout the network reliably outperforms d = 1 d=1 , and large blocks are clearly worse; the one placement that helps, symmetric positive-definite factors on the query and key projections, loses its small gain as models grow. At d = 1 d=1 , the constraint reduces to sphere optimization, with each row direction on its own unit sphere, which by itself already improves on tuned Muon. The same two findings hold for a diffusion transformer trained on ImageNet, and after fine-tuning, downstream accuracy does not separate the parameterizations. Our conclusion is that, across the realizations we tried, orthogonality between rows does not help language-model pre-training beyond sphere optimization. Since this appears to conflict with several prior results, we re-examine five prior methods in pre-training and fine-tuning that report orthogonality improvements. re-examine five prior methods in pre-training and fine-tuning that report orthogonality improvements. In each case the reported gain is attributable to numerical precision, training horizon, optimizer realization, or per-row norm control rather than to the orthogonality the methods impose.

Before the rise of large language models (LLMs), weight orthogonality was used to keep networks with millions of parameters well conditioned and their feature directions nonredundant ( Cissé et al., 2017 ; Huang et al., 2018 ) . For modern pretrained models, orthogonal fine-tuning methods report gains from learning orthogonal transformations of pretrained weights ( Qiu et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2024b ; Wu et al., 2026 ) or from constraining low-rank adapter factors to Stiefel manifolds ( Li et al., 2025 ) . In LLM pre-training, orthogonality has so far mostly shaped the training dynamics rather than the weights: the Muon optimizer ( Jordan et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) orthogonalizes the update to each weight matrix, and POET ( Qiu et al., 2025 ) learns orthogonal transformations of a fixed random weight matrix, preserving its singular values. Research blogs ( Bernstein, 2025 ; Su, 2025 ) derive optimizers that keep the weights themselves on the Stiefel manifold, without large-scale language-model experiments. Yoshihara (2026) evaluates this approach in GPT-2 models with up to 124M parameters and assigns different orthogonality structures to attention and MLP matrices. Whether keeping the weights themselves orthogonal helps LLM pre-training at scale remains open. We study this question systematically with decoder-only models from 360M to 3.1B parameters trained on nearly 200B tokens.

The most direct form of orthogonality training requires an entire weight matrix W ∈ ℝ m × n W\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} with m ≤ n m\leq n to have orthonormal rows, W ​ W ⊤ = I m WW^{\top}=I_{m} . This is a very strong regularization. It imposes m ⁡ ( m + 1 ) / 2 m(m+1)/2 constraints in total, so a square orthonormal matrix loses about half of its degrees of freedom, i.e., the number of effective parameters is roughly halved. We explored two routes for recovering the lost degrees of freedom. The first route relaxes the orthogonality constraint on W W to an orthogonal reparameterization of W W . The simplest variant adds per-row magnitudes: the model learns a row-orthonormal factor Q Q and a positive diagonal factor D D , and the effective weight is W = D ​ Q W=DQ . This reparameterization can represent every matrix whose rows are orthogonal and nonzero, but it recovers only m m degrees of freedom. Even with these magnitudes, full-matrix orthogonality substantially worsens validation loss, whether it is enforced by our projected update or by manifold Muon ( Bernstein, 2025 ) (Figure 1 ; Appendix M ). To go one step further, recall that every full-rank matrix admits a polar decomposition; we therefore replace the diagonal factor D D with a symmetric positive-definite (SPD) matrix S S , so that W = S ​ Q W=SQ . This reparameterization recovers all m ​ n mn degrees of freedom: S S contributes m ⁡ ( m + 1 ) / 2 m(m+1)/2 and Q Q contributes m ​ n − m ⁡ ( m + 1 ) / 2 mn-m(m+1)/2 . A triangular factor ( W = T ​ Q W=TQ ) and a singular-value form ( W = U ​ Σ ​ V ⊤ W=U\Sigma V^{\top} ) are equally expressive, but in training they recover much less of the constraint penalty than SPD, and the singular-value form recovers almost none.

• A pre-training study from 360M to 3.1B parameters showing that no block size above one used throughout the network improves on sphere optimization, that SPD factors on query and key projections give a small gain that vanishes as models grow, and that sphere optimization itself improves on tuned Muon; the same holds for a diffusion transformer on ImageNet, and fine-tuned models show no downstream advantage for any block size. • Re-examinations of five orthogonality methods in pre-training and fine-tuning that trace each reported gain to a factor other than orthogonality between rows.

The matched ladder covers 360M models at four budgets and reports C4 validation loss. Every pretraining cell uses three seeds, except the 16 × 16\times run (one) and 1.3B d = 1024 d=1024 SPD (two converged seeds). The AdamW learning rate for embedding/output-head parameters, normalization weights, and gains is shared rather than tuned across the Muon-family arms, so comparisons within the ladder are matched, whereas absolute gaps to Muon and MuonH are conditional on this setting; tuning only the gain learning rate improves d = 1 d=1 by up to 1.8 milli-loss (Appendix R ). In LLM pre-training, orthogonality has so far mostly shaped the training dynamics rather than the weights: the Muon optimizer ( Jordan et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) orthogonalizes the update to each weight matrix, and POET ( Qiu et al., 2025 ) learns orthogonal transformations of a fixed random weight matrix, preserving its singular values. Research blogs ( Bernstein, 2025 ; Su, 2025 ) derive optimizers that keep the weights themselves on the Stiefel manifold, without large-scale language-model experiments. Yoshihara (2026) evaluates this approach in GPT-2 models with up to 124M parameters and assigns different orthogonality structures to attention and MLP matrices. Whether keeping the weights themselves orthogonal helps LLM pre-training at scale remains open. We study this question systematically with decoder-only models from 360M to 3.1B parameters trained on nearly 200B tokens.

The most direct form of orthogonality training requires an entire weight matrix W ∈ ℝ m × n W\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} with m ≤ n m\leq n to have orthonormal rows, W ​ W ⊤ = I m WW^{\top}=I_{m} . This is a very strong regularization. It imposes m ⁡ ( m + 1 ) / 2 m(m+1)/2 constraints in total, so a square orthonormal matrix loses about half of its degrees of freedom, i.e., the number of effective parameters is roughly halved. We explored two routes for recovering the lost degrees of freedom. The first route relaxes the orthogonality constraint on W W to an orthogonal reparameterization of W W . The simplest variant adds per-row magnitudes: the model learns a row-orthonormal factor Q Q and a positive diagonal factor D D , and the effective weight is W = D ​ Q W=DQ . This reparameterization can represent every matrix whose rows are orthogonal and nonzero, but it recovers only m m degrees of freedom. Even with these magnitudes, full-matrix orthogonality substantially worsens validation loss, whether it is enforced by our projected update or by manifold Muon ( Bernstein, 2025 ) (Figure 1 ; Appendix M ). To go one step further, recall that every full-rank matrix admits a polar decomposition; we therefore replace the diagonal factor D D with a symmetric positive-definite (SPD) matrix S S , so that W = S ​ Q W=SQ . This reparameterization recovers all m ​ n mn degrees of freedom: S S contributes m ⁡ ( m + 1 ) / 2 m(m+1)/2 and Q Q contributes m ​ n − m ⁡ ( m + 1 ) / 2 mn-m(m+1)/2 . A triangular factor ( W = T ​ Q W=TQ ) and a singular-value form ( W = U ​ Σ ​ V ⊤ W=U\Sigma V^{\top} ) are equally expressive, but in training they recover much less of the constraint penalty than SPD, and the singular-value form recovers almost none.

The matched ladder covers 360M models at four budgets and reports C4 validation loss. Every pretraining cell uses three seeds, except the 16 × 16\times run (one) and 1.3B d = 1024 d=1024 SPD (two converged seeds). To count directions without the margin, we judge each truncation by how much it changes the network’s outputs. Our results point to compression as a signature of grokking rather than its cause. Every transformer memorizes its training data within 250 steps, but the steepest fall in the effective rank of W in W_{\text{in}} comes about 900 steps after the grokking onset, whether the onset occurs at step 6,500 or 21,000. Before the transition, no weight matrix can be truncated below 27–53 directions without changing the network’s outputs by more than 10%. After the transition, 8–13 directions suffice (Figure 1 b). We call this narrowing of the subspace that the outputs depend on subspace crystallization . It is consistent with the removal of memorizing components described by Nanda et al. (2023) . passages.section: What our measurements imply for rank analyses.
passages.text: Our results suggest four practices for measuring how many directions a network uses. First, count directions with a criterion that is independent of the margin, such as d out d_{\text{out}} , and compare the count with that of untrained or memorizing networks: in our MLP, d 0.99 d_{0.99} reported a narrowing that the outputs did not undergo. Second, report the training step with every count: the MLP’s d 0.99 d_{0.99} grows from 65 to 89 after generalization, so it is not a fixed property of the trained model. Third, compare any intervention that imposes low rank with a control of the same parameterization: against the unfactorized MLP, rank caps would wrongly appear to accelerate grokking. Fourth, read weight-spectrum statistics such as IPR or effective rank as signals of grokking only next to negative controls, since they also move in networks that never grok. In the transformer, a few leading singular directions of each matrix carry the solution and truncating to them keeps the test accuracy, while random truncations of equal rank do not (Table 15 , subject to the assumptions in Appendix D.3 ). In the MLP, one seed’s hidden representation transfers to another after an orthogonal alignment fitted on its few thousand training inputs, although their weight subspaces overlap no more than random ones (§ 5 ).

We asked whether rank compression causes grokking (Q1) and whether the learned solution comes to lie in a few directions of each weight matrix (Q2). The success of large language models in real-world applications relies on parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods such as Low-Rank Adaptation ( LoRA ), which inserts compact, trainable adapters into selected layers. In this paper, we propose SimplexLoRA , a LoRA variant that adaptively adjusts adapter ranks during fine-tuning based on their learned importance. Unlike standard LoRA , which employs a fixed rank across all layers, SimplexLoRA optimizes per-adapter importance weights on the n n -scaled simplex during a short warm-up and then freezes them, dynamically allocating capacity where it is most beneficial without increasing the overall parameter budget or inference cost. We evaluate SimplexLoRA across 12 language understanding, summarization, and reasoning tasks using DeBERTaV3, BART-large, Llama 3.1 8B, and Qwen3-8B. Our results show that SimplexLoRA consistently matches or outperforms standard LoRA and recent adaptive baselines, with the largest gains at low ranks. Our code is available at https://github.com/brain-lab-research/SimplexLoRA .

LoRA [ Hu et al., 2021 ] is a widely used parameter-efficient fine-tuning method [ Han et al., 2024 ] that parameterizes weight updates as 𝑾 ′ = 𝑾 0 + 𝑨 ​ 𝑩 {\bm{W}}^{\prime}={\bm{W}}^{0}+{\bm{A}}{\bm{B}} , with 𝑾 0 ∈ ℝ m × d {\bm{W}}^{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d} frozen and trainable 𝑨 ∈ ℝ m × r , 𝑩 ∈ ℝ r × d {\bm{A}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r},{\bm{B}}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d} , r ≪ m , d r\ll m,d . This approach achieves low inference overhead and substantially reduces memory during fine-tuning. Figure 1: SimplexLoRA framework. Per-adapter importance weights are constrained to the n n -scaled simplex, enabling dynamic allocation of a fixed rank budget across layers. Despite its efficiency, standard LoRA uses a fixed rank across all layers, ignoring layer-wise differences in convergence and representation learning. Existing adaptive rank allocation methods attempt to address this issue but suffer from the critical drawbacks: (i) substantially more trainable parameters [ Sheng et al., 2025 ] , (ii) non-negligible inference-time overhead caused by dynamic pruning or gating mechanisms [ Zhang et al., 2025 ] , and (iii) deviations from the standard LoRA pipeline that hinder compatibility [ Zhang et al., 2023b ] . See Section 2 for further discussion. To address this limitation, we propose SimplexLoRA , which assigns an importance weight to each of the n n LoRA adapters, constrained to the n n -scaled simplex to enforce a fixed parameter budget. Key properties: (i) ranks learned automatically during fine-tuning; (ii) simplex constraint preserves the LoRA parameter budget; (iii) full LoRA compatibility; (iv) negligible training and inference overhead.

We benchmark against baselines in default configurations under a number of training iterations. These span foundational PEFT methods (a performance floor) and recent dynamic-rank methods comparable to SimplexLoRA : Standard PEFT methods: LoRA [ Hu et al., 2021 ] , LoHA [ Nam et al., 2022 ] , Krona [ Edalati et al., 2022 ] , rsLoRA [ Kalajdzievski, 2023 ] , DoRA [ Liu et al., 2024 ] , and VERA [ Kopiczko et al., 2023 ] . Dynamic rank methods: AdaLoRA [ Zhang et al., 2023b ] , NormAL LoRA [ Aastik et al., 2025 ] , ElaLoRA [ Chang et al., 2025 ] , and FlexLoRA [ Liu et al., 2026 ] . In this setting (Table 1 ), where adapters are applied only to self-attention layers, full fine-tuning, standard LoRA , and SimplexLoRA emerge as the most robust methods, with SimplexLoRA achieving the best average score at the same 0.24 % 0.24\% parameter budget as standard LoRA . Other approaches require extensive hyperparameter tuning to achieve competitive performance. Consequently, we select standard LoRA as our primary baseline for further detailed comparison due to its widespread adoption and stability. Under tensor parallelism (TP) or fully sharded data parallelism (FSDP), matrix-aware optimizers such as Muon introduce communication to perform global matrix operations across shards. We propose Dobb ( D istributed O ptimizer with B lock-diagonal Eigen b ases), a matrix-aware optimizer designed to compute updates locally within parameter shards. Dobb approximates the input-activation second moment with diagonal blocks and tracks a complete basis within each block. Language-model scaling increases the memory requirements for parameters, gradients, and optimizer state ( Kaplan et al., 2020 ; Rajbhandari et al., 2020 ) . When these quantities exceed a single GPU’s capacity, training distributes them across devices through tensor parallelism (TP) or fully sharded data parallelism (FSDP) ( Shoeybi et al., 2019 ; Zhao et al., 2023 ) . Under either layout, each device holds one part of every sharded weight matrix, and we call this part a shard; data-parallel replicas hold copies of the same shards. Cross-shard communication is communication among the devices that hold different shards of one matrix. These layouts make matrix-aware optimization a distributed problem: an update defined on a complete weight matrix may require information held by several devices. Muon orthogonalizes momentum ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) , which introduces dense optimizer-specific communication in conventional sharded implementations ( Ahn et al., 2025 ; Khaled et al., 2026 ) . MuonBP reduces communication by performing local Newton–Schulz orthogonalization between periodic global steps, but those global steps still require full cross-shard communication ( Khaled et al., 2026 ) . The frequency of global orthogonalization controls the tradeoff between communication cost and optimization quality. Another approach, Dion, reduces the size of each exchange by approximating momentum with low-rank factors and retaining the residual through error feedback ( Ahn et al., 2025 ) . Its optimizer step communicates these factors across shards, so communication scales with the update rank.

In this work, we introduce Dobb ( D istributed O ptimizer with B lock-diagonal Eigen b ases) to reduce optimizer communication. We approximate the activation second moment by a block-diagonal matrix and retain a complete eigenbasis within every block. This construction discards cross-block correlations without imposing a reduced-rank constraint on the update. When these blocks align with shard boundaries, the optimizer step requires no cross-shard communication beyond the data-parallel synchronization of the activation second moments. Dion derives its low-rank factors from momentum; we instead project momentum onto an input-side basis from an exponentially averaged activation second moment, normalize the coefficients, and reconstruct the update. For a mini-batch gradient, projection into its own activation eigenbasis separates input spectral scales from the output-gradient structure, leaving the latter in the coefficients (Section 3 ). In our GPT-2 Small experiments, activation second moments exhibit greater spectral concentration than output-gradient second moments in most matched matrices (Figure 2 ). This motivates using the activation eigenbasis to expose the more concentrated factor’s directional scaling for normalization (Appendix F.2 ).

We introduce Dobb, which normalizes momentum coefficients in block-diagonal activation second-moment eigenbases. The central design choice is to discard cross-block correlations while retaining every basis direction within each block. Together with element-wise sign normalization, this construction introduces zero optimizer-specific cross-shard bytes when each block lies within one shard, beyond the data-parallel synchronization of the block second moments. Across GPT-2 Small, Medium, Large, and XL, Dobb exhibits less validation-loss degradation under block partitioning than Dion under corresponding rank reductions. Dobb’s optimizer call is shorter than those of Muon and Dion in every measured FSDP and TP configuration (Appendix G ). These timing runs are short and report pooled iteration times. Further work could investigate how block size and basis-refresh frequency should vary across layers and training stages. Because Dobb’s basis refresh reads no gradient, it could also move out of the optimizer call into idle intervals of forward-backward computation and communication (Appendix G.2 ). Understanding how discarded cross-block correlations and coefficient normalization theoretically affect optimization could also guide block partitions that preserve useful structure while respecting shard boundaries.

candidates.abstract_excerpt: The success of large language models in real-world applications relies on parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods such as Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), which inserts compact, trainable adapters into selected layers. In this paper, we propose SimplexLoRA, a LoRA variant that adaptively adjusts adapter ranks during fine-tuning based on their learned importance. Unlike standard LoRA, which employs a fixed rank across all layers, SimplexLoRA optimizes per-adapter importance weights on the $n$-scaled simplex during a short warm-up and then freezes them, dynamically allocating capacity where it is most beneficial without increasing the overall parameter budget or inference cost. We evaluate SimplexLoRA across 12 language understanding, summarization, and reasoning tasks using DeBERTaV3, BART-large, Llama 3.1 8B, and Qwen3-8B. Our results show that SimplexLoRA consistently matches or outperforms standard LoRA and recent adaptive baselines, with the largest gains at low ranks. Our code is available at https://github.com/brain-lab-research/SimplexLoRA.

candidates.title: EnergyCal: Taming Loss Spikes in Muon-Family Optimizers for Sparse MoE Training
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) language-model training can exhibit large loss spikes with Muon-family optimizers. We introduce EnergyCal, a lightweight rule that attenuates routed-expert updates according to the normalized squared Frobenius norm of their finite-step Newton-Schulz directions. EnergyCal leaves the spectral transform unchanged and adds no persistent optimizer state. We evaluate it on a 4B-parameter MoE model. Against a development-selected, lower-learning-rate MuonH recipe, EnergyCal-MuonH reduces mean thresholded loss-spike burden by 99.51% and final geometric-mean perplexity by 4.06%, with a modest throughput cost. With plain Muon at matched nominal learning rate and weight decay, the reduction in mean spike burden averages 95.98% across the two tested exponents, accompanied by small endpoint improvements. These findings support stabilization both with and without Hyperball in the evaluated setting.

We present SparseLift, a low-overhead compiler for the sparse path of large-scale recommendation training. candidates.title: A knowledge-driven nonconvex square-root regularization framework for joint group sparsity and structured smoothness
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Structured sparse learning is a leading paradigm for high-dimensional data modeling, as it enables rigorous integration of domain-validated structural priors into the learning process. Among these priors, pre-defined grouped structure and piecewise smoothness are ubiquitous in real-world applications. However, most existing structured regularization methods are built on squared loss and convex penalties, rarely jointly model these two complementary structural priors, and suffer from two key limitations. Their optimal tuning parameters are sensitive to the unknown noise level $σ$ due to the squared loss. Meanwhile, convex penalties induce inherent estimation bias and severe over-shrinkage of large magnitudes. candidates.title: Improving the Optimization Landscape of Matrix Completion with $ε$-close Surrogates
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Non-convex optimization is central to machine learning and AI, yet unlike its convex counterpart, it still lacks a general and principled framework. In this work, we try to highlight the importance of combining noisy perturbations with over-parametrization mathematically under the classic setting of matrix completion (MC). Matrix completion is an important non-convex recovery problem in which only a subset of a matrix's entries is observed, and the remaining entries must be recovered using low-rank constraints. This problem is notoriously difficult because observations are limited. However, we show that by injecting $ε$-level perturbations into the nullspace of the observation mask, we can construct noisy matrix sensing surrogates whose solutions remain $\mathcal{O}(ε)$-close to the ground truth with valid restricted isometry property (RIP) constants. The existence of RIP further enables powerful tensor frameworks to be applied with theoretical guarantees. This approach reflects a broader empirical trend in which stochasticity or noise improves the curvature of the optimization landscape, allowing over-parameterized (a.k.a large) models to better separate signal from noise. passages.text: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) enables parameter-efficient fine-tuning but can suffer from redundant basis directions. Constraining the basis factor to the Stiefel manifold addresses this redundancy through orthonormality. Landing methods allow temporarily infeasible iterates to explore a neighborhood of the manifold while progressively restoring orthogonality without per-step retractions. To improve optimization efficiency while retaining this flexibility, we introduce ProLand (Product-space Landing), a retraction-free optimizer that combines coordinated factor updates with Muon-style spectral directions. By designing the updates in the space of the represented weight increment, ProLand separates objective optimization from orthogonality restoration, supporting efficient feasibility recovery. This coordinated construction also enables Muon-style directions to guide objective optimization while preserving that separation. Experiments cover four GLUE validation tasks on DeBERTa-v3-base and seven language benchmarks on Qwen2.5-3B, Llama-3.2-3B, and Moonlight-16B-A3B across multiple adapter ranks. Across these 11 tasks, ProLand achieves the highest average score among the compared methods in every tested encoder and decoder model–rank configuration.

We design the joint first-order change D B ​ A + B ​ D A D_{B}A+BD_{A} in the represented weight increment and realize it through factor directions satisfying B ⊤ ​ D B = 0 B^{\top}D_{B}=0 , even when B B is infeasible. passages.text: A growing body of work reports benefits from orthogonality constraints in fine-tuning large language models (LLMs). These results raise an open question: do orthogonality constraints also help LLM pre-training? We conduct a systematic empirical study of decoder-only LLM pre-training with models ranging from 360M to 3.1B parameters, trained on nearly 200B tokens. We examine fourteen variants of orthogonality training: some constrain the weight matrix itself, while others use orthogonal factors to reparameterize it. Because a strictly orthogonal square matrix loses half of its degrees of freedom, we also study block-wise orthogonality, where every d d rows form a row-orthonormal (Stiefel) matrix and the block size d d is a hyperparameter. Among block sizes ranging from 1 to the shorter side of the matrix, no d > 1 d>1 used throughout the network reliably outperforms d = 1 d=1 , and large blocks are clearly worse; the one placement that helps, symmetric positive-definite factors on the query and key projections, loses its small gain as models grow. At d = 1 d=1 , the constraint reduces to sphere optimization, with each row direction on its own unit sphere, which by itself already improves on tuned Muon. The same two findings hold for a diffusion transformer trained on ImageNet, and after fine-tuning, downstream accuracy does not separate the parameterizations. Our conclusion is that, across the realizations we tried, orthogonality between rows does not help language-model pre-training beyond sphere optimization. Since this appears to conflict with several prior results, we re-examine five prior methods in pre-training and fine-tuning that report orthogonality improvements. re-examine five prior methods in pre-training and fine-tuning that report orthogonality improvements. In each case the reported gain is attributable to numerical precision, training horizon, optimizer realization, or per-row norm control rather than to the orthogonality the methods impose.

Before the rise of large language models (LLMs), weight orthogonality was used to keep networks with millions of parameters well conditioned and their feature directions nonredundant ( Cissé et al., 2017 ; Huang et al., 2018 ) . For modern pretrained models, orthogonal fine-tuning methods report gains from learning orthogonal transformations of pretrained weights ( Qiu et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2024b ; Wu et al., 2026 ) or from constraining low-rank adapter factors to Stiefel manifolds ( Li et al., 2025 ) . In LLM pre-training, orthogonality has so far mostly shaped the training dynamics rather than the weights: the Muon optimizer ( Jordan et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) orthogonalizes the update to each weight matrix, and POET ( Qiu et al., 2025 ) learns orthogonal transformations of a fixed random weight matrix, preserving its singular values. Research blogs ( Bernstein, 2025 ; Su, 2025 ) derive optimizers that keep the weights themselves on the Stiefel manifold, without large-scale language-model experiments. Yoshihara (2026) evaluates this approach in GPT-2 models with up to 124M parameters and assigns different orthogonality structures to attention and MLP matrices. Whether keeping the weights themselves orthogonal helps LLM pre-training at scale remains open. We study this question systematically with decoder-only models from 360M to 3.1B parameters trained on nearly 200B tokens.

The most direct form of orthogonality training requires an entire weight matrix W ∈ ℝ m × n W\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} with m ≤ n m\leq n to have orthonormal rows, W ​ W ⊤ = I m WW^{\top}=I_{m} . This is a very strong regularization. It imposes m ⁡ ( m + 1 ) / 2 m(m+1)/2 constraints in total, so a square orthonormal matrix loses about half of its degrees of freedom, i.e., the number of effective parameters is roughly halved. We explored two routes for recovering the lost degrees of freedom. The first route relaxes the orthogonality constraint on W W to an orthogonal reparameterization of W W . The simplest variant adds per-row magnitudes: the model learns a row-orthonormal factor Q Q and a positive diagonal factor D D , and the effective weight is W = D ​ Q W=DQ . This reparameterization can represent every matrix whose rows are orthogonal and nonzero, but it recovers only m m degrees of freedom. Even with these magnitudes, full-matrix orthogonality substantially worsens validation loss, whether it is enforced by our projected update or by manifold Muon ( Bernstein, 2025 ) (Figure 1 ; Appendix M ). To go one step further, recall that every full-rank matrix admits a polar decomposition; we therefore replace the diagonal factor D D with a symmetric positive-definite (SPD) matrix S S , so that W = S ​ Q W=SQ . This reparameterization recovers all m ​ n mn degrees of freedom: S S contributes m ⁡ ( m + 1 ) / 2 m(m+1)/2 and Q Q contributes m ​ n − m ⁡ ( m + 1 ) / 2 mn-m(m+1)/2 . A triangular factor ( W = T ​ Q W=TQ ) and a singular-value form ( W = U ​ Σ ​ V ⊤ W=U\Sigma V^{\top} ) are equally expressive, but in training they recover much less of the constraint penalty than SPD, and the singular-value form recovers almost none.

passages.text: Our results suggest four practices for measuring how many directions a network uses. First, count directions with a criterion that is independent of the margin, such as d out d_{\text{out}} , and compare the count with that of untrained or memorizing networks: in our MLP, d 0.99 d_{0.99} reported a narrowing that the outputs did not undergo. Second, report the training step with every count: the MLP’s d 0.99 d_{0.99} grows from 65 to 89 after generalization, so it is not a fixed property of the trained model. Third, compare any intervention that imposes low rank with a control of the same parameterization: against the unfactorized MLP, rank caps would wrongly appear to accelerate grokking. Fourth, read weight-spectrum statistics such as IPR or effective rank as signals of grokking only next to negative controls, since they also move in networks that never grok. In the transformer, a few leading singular directions of each matrix carry the solution and truncating to them keeps the test accuracy, while random truncations of equal rank do not (Table 15 , subject to the assumptions in Appendix D.3 ). In the MLP, one seed’s hidden representation transfers to another after an orthogonal alignment fitted on its few thousand training inputs, although their weight subspaces overlap no more than random ones (§ 5 ).

We asked whether rank compression causes grokking (Q1) and whether the learned solution comes to lie in a few directions of each weight matrix (Q2). For Q1, compression follows the grokking onset rather than memorization: it tracks the onset across a threefold range of onset times while the training set is memorized within 250 steps, it does not start before test accuracy rises, and forcing low rank from initialization does not bring grokking forward. Compression is therefore a signature of grokking rather than its cause. For Q2, the answer depends on how directions are counted. Judged by the outputs, the transformer crystallizes during the transition, to 8–13 directions per matrix, at the same time as its memorizing components are removed. The MLP trained with mean-squared error does not: its d 0.99 d_{0.99} narrows only because its margins grow, and its late compression tracks the optimizer’s effective learning rate. Counting directions by the outputs rather than by accuracy, and comparing any imposed low rank with a control of the same parameterization, is what makes these distinctions visible.

The resulting update is orthogonal to the current weights in the Frobenius inner product. This orthogonality eliminates the first-order increase in the weight norm, so the norm grows only at second order in the step size. With bounded directions and a constant nominal learning rate, this guarantees O ⁡ ( t ) O(\sqrt{t}) norm growth and C T = Ω ⁡ ( T ) C_{T}=\Omega(\sqrt{T}) , with the same accumulation order over later training windows. MuonGS thus improves vanilla Muon’s worst-case accumulation guarantee without fixing a radius. For smooth scale-invariant objectives, we further established the convergence rate for MuonGS. We evaluate MuonGS on FineWeb pretraining with modernized GPT-style models of approximately 160M and 400M parameters. At longer training horizons, MuonGS achieves lower validation perplexity than MuonH. Fitting MuonH’s loss as a function of the training-token budget gives an estimated token-equivalent speedup of up to about 15 % 15\% at matched validation loss. In addition, MuonGS obtains lower validation perplexity than MuonH when pretraining a modern MoE model, having about 135M active and 1B total parameters, on Ultra-FineWeb. These results support MuonGS as a practical optimizer and demonstrate the value of relaxing norm-control requirements. Together with our theoretical guarantees, these findings provide a positive answer to the question above by showing that weaker norm control can indeed sustain accumulation throughout training while improving empirical performance. Our analysis bounds relative weight displacement and, under scale-invariance and Lipschitz assumptions, attainable loss change. At a constant nominal learning rate, it distinguishes vanilla Muon’s logarithmic worst case from the linear guarantees of MuonW and fixed-norm control. Serving many LoRA adapters under a shared resource budget turns post-hoc compression into a two-level allocation problem: rank must be distributed across layers within each adapter and across adapters within the fleet. Although trained LoRAs contain substantial spectral redundancy, spectral reconstruction alone does not determine how much compression an adapter can functionally tolerate. We formulate fleet compression through a functional rank–distortion frontier for each adapter, followed by fleet-level minimax allocation under a shared rank budget. Given exact frontiers, this decomposition is equivalent to joint optimization over all layer ranks. We introduce Functional Rank Allocation (FRA) , an unlabeled method for constructing practical frontiers. FRA measures isolated module truncations end to end, uses these measurements as an additive search surrogate solved by dynamic programming, remeasures every complete candidate, and takes the lower-risk envelope with a complementary spectral proposal before exact minimax allocation over the constructed frontiers. Across 78 adapters from three public fleets, FRA improves worst-case and tail utility over uniform spectral compression in constrained-budget regimes. Fixed-budget probes show that isolated costs rank candidates well, but their calibration shifts across proposal shapes; end-to-end verification and the spectral proposal therefore limit functional-search error.

To characterize rank redundancy in the wild, we analyze 96,370 96{,}370 matrices from 200 popular LoRA repositories on Hugging Face and find that spectral energy is strongly concentrated: at τ = .90 \tau=.90 , the median layer retains only 31.2 % 31.2\% of its nominal rank (Fig. 1 ). Within a single adapter, different layers need not tolerate the same degree of truncation. At fleet scale, the problem becomes coupled, as adapters share the same serving capacity yet may differ substantially in how much compression they can tolerate. The success of large language models in real-world applications relies on parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods such as Low-Rank Adaptation ( LoRA ), which inserts compact, trainable adapters into selected layers. In this paper, we propose SimplexLoRA , a LoRA variant that adaptively adjusts adapter ranks during fine-tuning based on their learned importance. Unlike standard LoRA , which employs a fixed rank across all layers, SimplexLoRA optimizes per-adapter importance weights on the n n -scaled simplex during a short warm-up and then freezes them, dynamically allocating capacity where it is most beneficial without increasing the overall parameter budget or inference cost. We evaluate SimplexLoRA across 12 language understanding, summarization, and reasoning tasks using DeBERTaV3, BART-large, Llama 3.1 8B, and Qwen3-8B. Our results show that SimplexLoRA consistently matches or outperforms standard LoRA and recent adaptive baselines, with the largest gains at low ranks. Our code is available at https://github.com/brain-lab-research/SimplexLoRA .

LoRA [ Hu et al., 2021 ] is a widely used parameter-efficient fine-tuning method [ Han et al., 2024 ] that parameterizes weight updates as 𝑾 ′ = 𝑾 0 + 𝑨 ​ 𝑩 {\bm{W}}^{\prime}={\bm{W}}^{0}+{\bm{A}}{\bm{B}} , with 𝑾 0 ∈ ℝ m × d {\bm{W}}^{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d} frozen and trainable 𝑨 ∈ ℝ m × r , 𝑩 ∈ ℝ r × d {\bm{A}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r},{\bm{B}}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d} , r ≪ m , d r\ll m,d . This approach achieves low inference overhead and substantially reduces memory during fine-tuning. Figure 1: SimplexLoRA framework. Per-adapter importance weights are constrained to the n n -scaled simplex, enabling dynamic allocation of a fixed rank budget across layers. Despite its efficiency, standard LoRA uses a fixed rank across all layers, ignoring layer-wise differences in convergence and representation learning. Existing adaptive rank allocation methods attempt to address this issue but suffer from the critical drawbacks: (i) substantially more trainable parameters [ Sheng et al., 2025 ] , (ii) non-negligible inference-time overhead caused by dynamic pruning or gating mechanisms [ Zhang et al., 2025 ] , and (iii) deviations from the standard LoRA pipeline that hinder compatibility [ Zhang et al., 2023b ] . See Section 2 for further discussion. To address this limitation, we propose SimplexLoRA , which assigns an importance weight to each of the n n LoRA adapters, constrained to the n n -scaled simplex to enforce a fixed parameter budget. Key properties: (i) ranks learned automatically during fine-tuning; (ii) simplex constraint preserves the LoRA parameter budget; (iii) full LoRA compatibility; (iv) negligible training and inference overhead.

We benchmark against baselines in default configurations under a number of training iterations. These span foundational PEFT methods (a performance floor) and recent dynamic-rank methods comparable to SimplexLoRA : Standard PEFT methods: LoRA [ Hu et al., 2021 ] , LoHA [ Nam et al., 2022 ] , Krona [ Edalati et al., 2022 ] , rsLoRA [ Kalajdzievski, 2023 ] , DoRA [ Liu et al., 2024 ] , and VERA [ Kopiczko et al., 2023 ] . Dynamic rank methods: AdaLoRA [ Zhang et al., 2023b ] , NormAL LoRA [ Aastik et al., 2025 ] , ElaLoRA [ Chang et al., 2025 ] , and FlexLoRA [ Liu et al., 2026 ] . In this setting (Table 1 ), where adapters are applied only to self-attention layers, full fine-tuning, standard LoRA , and SimplexLoRA emerge as the most robust methods, with SimplexLoRA achieving the best average score at the same 0.24 % 0.24\% parameter budget as standard LoRA . Other approaches require extensive hyperparameter tuning to achieve competitive performance. Consequently, we select standard LoRA as our primary baseline for further detailed comparison due to its widespread adoption and stability. Language-model scaling increases the memory requirements for parameters, gradients, and optimizer state ( Kaplan et al., 2020 ; Rajbhandari et al., 2020 ) . When these quantities exceed a single GPU’s capacity, training distributes them across devices through tensor parallelism (TP) or fully sharded data parallelism (FSDP) ( Shoeybi et al., 2019 ; Zhao et al., 2023 ) . Under either layout, each device holds one part of every sharded weight matrix, and we call this part a shard; data-parallel replicas hold copies of the same shards. Cross-shard communication is communication among the devices that hold different shards of one matrix. These layouts make matrix-aware optimization a distributed problem: an update defined on a complete weight matrix may require information held by several devices. Muon orthogonalizes momentum ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) , which introduces dense optimizer-specific communication in conventional sharded implementations ( Ahn et al., 2025 ; Khaled et al., 2026 ) . MuonBP reduces communication by performing local Newton–Schulz orthogonalization between periodic global steps, but those global steps still require full cross-shard communication ( Khaled et al., 2026 ) . The frequency of global orthogonalization controls the tradeoff between communication cost and optimization quality. Another approach, Dion, reduces the size of each exchange by approximating momentum with low-rank factors and retaining the residual through error feedback ( Ahn et al., 2025 ) . Its optimizer step communicates these factors across shards, so communication scales with the update rank.

In this work, we introduce Dobb ( D istributed O ptimizer with B lock-diagonal Eigen b ases) to reduce optimizer communication. We approximate the activation second moment by a block-diagonal matrix and retain a complete eigenbasis within every block. This construction discards cross-block correlations without imposing a reduced-rank constraint on the update. When these blocks align with shard boundaries, the optimizer step requires no cross-shard communication beyond the data-parallel synchronization of the activation second moments. Dion derives its low-rank factors from momentum; we instead project momentum onto an input-side basis from an exponentially averaged activation second moment, normalize the coefficients, and reconstruct the update. For a mini-batch gradient, projection into its own activation eigenbasis separates input spectral scales from the output-gradient structure, leaving the latter in the coefficients (Section 3 ). In our GPT-2 Small experiments, activation second moments exhibit greater spectral concentration than output-gradient second moments in most matched matrices (Figure 2 ). This motivates using the activation eigenbasis to expose the more concentrated factor’s directional scaling for normalization (Appendix F.2 ).

We introduce Dobb, which normalizes momentum coefficients in block-diagonal activation second-moment eigenbases. The central design choice is to discard cross-block correlations while retaining every basis direction within each block. Together with element-wise sign normalization, this construction introduces zero optimizer-specific cross-shard bytes when each block lies within one shard, beyond the data-parallel synchronization of the block second moments. Across GPT-2 Small, Medium, Large, and XL, Dobb exhibits less validation-loss degradation under block partitioning than Dion under corresponding rank reductions. Because Dobb’s basis refresh reads no gradient, it could also move out of the optimizer call into idle intervals of forward-backward computation and communication (Appendix G.2 ). Understanding how discarded cross-block correlations and coefficient normalization theoretically affect optimization could also guide block partitions that preserve useful structure while respecting shard boundaries.
